events.title: Earliest published cabaret songs
events.label: 1926 · Earliest published cabaret songs
events.shortDescription: Kaper’s Warsaw cabaret songs appear in print under the pseudonym Bruno Asper, which the manuscripts show him already using in 1923.
events.longDescription: Songs for Warsaw cabarets published under the pseudonym Bruno Asper, to words by Andrzej Włast. The printed editions of 1926 are the earliest published songs documented here; the signature itself is older, appearing on the 1923 manuscript of Koszutski Girls.

image.altText: Black-and-white stage photograph of Zula Pogorzelska posing with a folding fan in an ornate costume and large decorative hat.

events.title: Meeting Walter Jurmann
events.label: 1931 · Meeting Walter Jurmann
events.shortDescription: Fritz Rotter pairs Kaper with Walter Jurmann in 1931, at the start of the partnership that shapes his European film career.
events.longDescription: Fritz Rotter paired the two composers in 1931, when each had already had separate successes and sound film was multiplying commissions. Their names first stand together in the credits of Die große Attraktion, directed by Max Reichmann, but three of the film’s songs were registered under Kaper’s name alone: “Du warst mir ein Roman”, the slow fox written for Richard Tauber, “Das verliebte Orchester” and “Ich steh’ im Schnee und wart’ auf dich”. The first film signed jointly throughout is Ehe mit beschränkter Haftung.

image.altText: Photograph of Bronisław Kaper with Walter Jurmann.

events.title: Hollywood debut
events.label: 1935 · Hollywood debut
events.shortDescription: Kaper makes his Hollywood debut at MGM, contributing to Escapade and other major studio projects.
events.longDescription: The first American score documented here is “Escapade” (dir. Robert Z. Leonard) with William Powell and Luise Rainer. Press hails “Two New Composers” of Kiepura’s European hits. Songs also for Marx Brothers’ “A Night at the Opera” (with Ned Washington) and “Mutiny on the Bounty”. MGM engaged Kaper at first as a song specialist rather than as a film composer, and by his own account he moved only gradually from songwriter to composer of scores. For Escapade, which opened in July 1935, he supplied a single number, “You’re All I Need”, to words by Gus Kahn.

image.altText: Sheet-music cover for “You’re All I Need” from the MGM film Escapade (1935).
